entities.name: Harivarman II
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Harivarman II, who reigned as King of Champa from approximately 989 CE until his death in 997 CE, marked a pivotal period of resilience and strategic realignment for the ancient Cham kingdom amidst escalating pressures from the expanding Đại Việt (Vietnamese) state. Succeeding the brief and tumultuous reign of Parameshvaravarman I, Harivarman II ascended to a throne challenged by internal instability and external aggression, notably the devastating Đại Việt invasion of 982 CE that sacked the Cham capital Indrapura. His rule, though relatively short, was characterized by determined efforts to restore Cham sovereignty and cultural identity in the face of persistent northern encroachment, temporarily shifting the kingdom's political center southward.

Following the catastrophic Đại Việt invasion under Emperor Lê Hoàn, which resulted in the death of Parameshvaravarman I and the destruction of Indrapura, Harivarman II successfully consolidated Cham authority. He moved the royal capital from Indrapura (near modern Đà Nẵng) further south to Vijaya (modern Bình Định province), a more defensible location that would serve as the Cham capital for centuries. This strategic relocation, occurring around 989 CE, was not merely a retreat but a deliberate act to re-establish a secure base, rebuild state infrastructure, and mobilize forces. His reign saw the re-assertion of Cham political and military strength, albeit in a modified geographic configuration, preparing the kingdom for future confrontations.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Harivarman II's strategic relocation of the Cham capital to Vijaya ensured the kingdom's survival and allowed it to remain an independent regional power for another five centuries. His leadership stabilized Champa after a devastating invasion, fundamentally reshaping its political and military geography.
